source_text: Quoniam de secunda natiuitate diximus, qua se hominibus in carne monstrauit, ueniamus ad opera illa miranda, quae cum essent caelestis indicia uirtutis, magum Iudaei putauerunt. cum primum coepit adolescere, tinctus est ab Iohanne propheta in Iordane flumine, ut lauacro spiritali peccata non sua, quae utique non habebat, sed carnis quam gerebat aboleret, ut quemadmodum Iudaeos suscepta circumcisione, sic etiam gentes baptismo id est purifici roris perfusione saluaret. tum uox audita de caelo est: filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. quae uox aput Dauid praedicta inuenitur. et descendit super eum spiritus dei formatus in specie columbae candidae. exinde maximas uirtutes coepit operari, non praestrigiis magicis, quae nihil ueri ac solidi ostentant, sed ui ac potestate caelesti: quae iam pridem prophetis nuntiantibus canebantur. quae opera tam multa sunt, ut unus liber ad conplectenda omnia satis non sit. enumerabo igitur illa breuiter atque generatim sine ulla personarum ac locorum designatione, ut ad exponendam passionis eius crucisque rationem possim peruenire, quo iam dudum festinat oratio. uirtutes eius fuerunt quas Apollo portentificas appellauit, quod quacumque iter faciebat, aegros ac debiles et omni morborum genere laborantes uno uerbo unoque momento reddebat incolumes, adeo ut membris omnibus capti receptis repente uiribus roborati ipsi lectulos suos reportarent, in quibus fuerant paulo ante delati. claudis uero ac pedum uitio adflictis non modo gradiendi, sed etiam currendi dabat facultatem. tum quorum caeca lumina in altissimis tenebris erant, eorum oculos in pristinum restituebat aspectum. mutorum quoque linguas in eloquium sermonemque soluebat item surdorum patefactis auribus insinuabat auditum, pollutos et aspersos maculis repurgabat. et haec omnia non manibus aut aliqua medella, sed uerbo ac iussione faciebat, sicut etiam Sibylla praedixerat: πάντα λόγῳ πράσσων πᾶσάν τε νόσον θεραπεύων nec utique mirum quod uerbo faceret mirabilia, cum ipse esset dei uerbum caelesti uirtute ac potestate subnixum. nec satis fuit quod uires inbecillis redderet, quod debilibus integritatem, quod aegris et languentibus sanitatem, nisi etiam mortuos suscitaret uelut e somno solutos ad uitamque reuocaret. quae uidentes tunc Iudaei daemonica potentia fieri arguebant, cum omnia sic futura ut facta sunt arcanae illorum litterae continerent.
pass_a_gloss: Since we have spoken about the second birth, by which He showed Himself to men in the flesh, let us come to those wonderful works, which, although they were heavenly signs of virtue, the Jews considered to be of a magician. When He first began to grow up, He was baptized by John the prophet in the Jordan river, so that by spiritual washing He might abolish not His own sins, which He certainly did not have, but those of the flesh which He bore, so that just as the Jews were saved by having received circumcision, so also the Gentiles might be saved by baptism, that is, by the pouring of purifying dew. Then a voice was heard from heaven: You are my Son, I have begotten You today. This voice is found to have been predicted by David. And the Spirit of God descended upon Him in the form of a white dove. From then on, He began to perform great virtues, not by magical tricks, which show nothing true and solid, but by heavenly power and virtue: which the prophets had long ago announced. These works are so many that one book is not enough to include them all. I will therefore briefly enumerate them in general, without any designation of persons or places, so that I may be able to come to the explanation of the reason for His passion and cross, to which my speech has been hastening for a long time. His virtues were what Apollo called portentific, because wherever He went, He restored the sick and the weak and those suffering from every kind of disease to health with one word and in one moment, so that those who had been captured by all their limbs and had suddenly been strengthened by regained powers carried their own stretchers, on which they had been carried a little while before. And to those who were afflicted by lameness or a defect of the feet, He not only gave the ability to walk but also to run. Then to those whose eyes were blind in the highest darkness, He restored their sight to its former state. He also loosened the tongues of the mute into speech and conversation, and to the deaf, with their ears opened, He introduced hearing. He purified the polluted and those sprinkled with stains. And He did all these things not with His hands or any medicine, but with His word and command, just as the Sibyl had also predicted: Doing all things with a word and healing every disease. And it is not surprising that He did wonderful things with a word, since He Himself was the Word of God, supported by heavenly virtue and power. And it was not enough that He restored strength to the weak, integrity to the feeble, and health to the sick and the languid, unless He also raised the dead, as if they had been freed from sleep and recalled to life. The Jews, seeing these things, argued that they were done by demonic power, although their secret writings contained all these things which were to happen just as they did.

bible_refs.note: You are my Son, I have begotten You today

pass_b_english: Having spoken of the second birth, by which He revealed Himself to humanity in the flesh, we now turn to those marvelous works which, though they were heavenly signs of power, the Jews dismissed as sorcery. When He first began to mature, He was baptized by the prophet John in the Jordan River, that by a spiritual washing He might cleanse not His own sins — for He had none — but the sins of the flesh He had assumed. He did this so that, just as the Jews were saved through the circumcision they received, so also the Gentiles might be saved through baptism, that is, through the sprinkling of purifying dew. Then a voice was heard from heaven: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you" (Psalm 2:7). This same voice had been foretold by David. And the Spirit of God descended upon Him in the form of a white dove. From that moment He began to perform mighty deeds, not by magical tricks that display nothing true or solid, but by heavenly power and authority — deeds the prophets had long ago proclaimed. These works are so numerous that no single book could contain them all. I will therefore enumerate them briefly and in general categories, without naming specific persons or places, so that I may arrive at the explanation of the meaning of His passion and cross, toward which my discourse has long been hastening.

His mighty works were what Apollo called "portentous," because wherever He went He restored the sick, the weak, and those suffering from every kind of disease to full health with a single word and in a single instant. The result was that people who had been completely paralyzed, suddenly strengthened by recovered power, picked up their own stretchers — the very beds on which they had been carried only a short time before — and carried them away. To those crippled or afflicted with defects of the feet He gave not only the ability to walk but even to run. To those whose eyes were blind in deepest darkness He restored their original sight. He loosened the tongues of the mute into speech and conversation, and to the deaf, with their ears opened, He gave hearing. He cleansed those defiled and sprinkled with stains. He did all these things not with His hands or any medicine, but with His word and command, just as the Sibyl had also predicted: "Doing all things by a word and healing every disease." Nor is it surprising that He performed wonders by a word, since He Himself is the Word of God, upheld by heavenly power and authority. It was not enough that He gave strength to the weak, soundness to the frail, and health to the sick and languishing; He also raised the dead, as if freeing them from sleep and recalling them to life. The Jews who witnessed these things charged that they were done by demonic power, even though their own secret writings contained all these events exactly as they came to pass.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that correctly identifies the Davidic prophecy as Psalm 2:7. The Sibylline Greek quote is correctly translated in both. All clauses, including the complex description of the healed limbs and the reference to the Jews' secret writings, are preserved.

The Latin text is correctly identified as Lactantius' Divine Institutes 4.15. The translation preserves the source's content, including all key arguments, quotations, and doctrinal points. The inline scripture citation (Psalm 2:7) is accurate. The term 'portentificas' is correctly translated as 'portentous' in Pass B, and the Sibyl's quote is accurately rendered. No omissions, additions, or distortions are found in the translation. The title 'Christ's Miraculous Works' appropriately reflects the content of the passage.
